thread.previously: Megaspeed, a Singapore firm, is suspected of funnelling Nvidia AI chips to China; it denies smuggling. Reports say CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive US officials believe works for Chinese intelligence. Nvidia opened an independent probe on 8 November. On 9 November the NYT reported Commerce halted its Megaspeed inquiry after Nvidia contacted agents; DOJ asked for the pause and runs a criminal inquiry. House chairs requested an 18 November briefing.
thread.changed: Huang resigned on 12 November, and Nvidia gave no official reason. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO and Harvey C. Jones became the first board chair. Shares swung sharply, and Huang agreed to testify before Congress.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang quits Nvidia; CFO Colette Kress steps in as interim CEO
stories.question: Why did Jensen Huang quit Nvidia, and who runs the AI chip leader now?
stories.dek: Nvidia gave no reason. Huang left after days of reports about his relationships and possible China security risks. Its chief financial officer now runs Nvidia while the board looks for a permanent boss.

so_far.text: Nvidia makes the chips that much of the world's AI runs on, and US rules limit what it may sell to China. Since October 2025, Singapore police have been investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore tech firm. Reports say it sent chips to data centres that may serve Chinese customers. Megaspeed denies this. On 8 November 2026 Jensen Huang admitted being unfaithful to his wife. Reports named Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. US intelligence officials consider her a Chinese spy, but this is alleged, not proven. Nvidia's board opened an investigation the same day.

what_happened.text: On 12 November 2026 Nvidia's board announced that co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. It gave no reason. Colette Kress, chief financial officer (CFO) since September 2013, became interim CEO and stays CFO. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO, became the board's first-ever chair. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO. Nvidia shares fell as much as 13–14% at the open, then closed down 4.34% at $166.19. Representative Brian Mast said Huang had agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, probably under oath, after being threatened with a subpoena.

steps.text: US export rules decide which AI chips Nvidia may sell to China, so every China sale is a security question.
Huang supported selling advanced chips to China, and that stance became politically sensitive after the December 2025 H200 approval.
Reports tied him to Alice Huang of Megaspeed, a firm suspected of moving chips; US officials allege she is a Chinese spy.
The New York Times reported a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a vice-president who reported to him; Reuters reported a third relationship, with another employee.
After calls in Washington for him to resign, the board announced his exit on 12 November without giving a reason.

history.text: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem on 5 April 1993. The company listed its shares on 22 January 1999. The China problem began in October 2022. That month, US rules restricted exports of advanced chips to China and put Nvidia's data-centre chip on the export control list. From then on, a sale to China needed Washington's approval. In November 2022 Nvidia responded with the A800, a version built to stay within the rules. In August 2025 Nvidia and AMD agreed to pay 15% of their China chip revenue to get export licences. Nvidia later stopped making its H20 chip after Beijing warned Chinese firms away from it. In October 2025 Singapore police began investigating Megaspeed. On 29 October 2025 Nvidia became the first company ever worth $5 trillion. In December 2025 President Trump approved H200 exports to China. That made Huang's support for selling chips to China politically sensitive. Pressure for tighter rules grew at the same time. In January 2026 the House passed the Remote Access Security Act. It would extend export controls to the remote use of computing power, and it still needs Senate approval. In August 2026 employees of Nvidia and Supermicro were indicted over smuggling AI servers to China. So when reports linked Huang personally to a former Megaspeed executive, the scandal touched the most sensitive part of Nvidia's business.

lesson.concept: How a board replaces a CEO overnight
lesson.big_idea: A company's board, not its CEO, hires and replaces the boss. If a CEO leaves suddenly, the board names a temporary leader at once, then searches for a permanent one.

steps.title: The board sits above the CEO
steps.text: Shareholders elect a board of directors. The board hires the chief executive (CEO), checks their work and can replace them. Jensen Huang was both CEO and a board member until 12 November 2026.

steps.title: A chair leads the board
steps.text: The board chair runs board meetings and speaks for the directors. Nvidia had no chair until 12 November 2026, when it named Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO.

steps.title: Name a temporary boss at once
steps.text: A company cannot pause, so the board names an interim CEO, meaning a temporary boss, often someone who knows the business. Nvidia chose Colette Kress, its CFO since September 2013. She stays CFO.

steps.title: Search for the permanent CEO
steps.text: The board then compares candidates and votes on one. Nvidia's board will consider internal and external candidates. It is not yet known who will be chosen, or when.

steps.title: Investors price the uncertainty
steps.text: Until the new leader is clear, investors must guess, so shares can drop hard, then partly recover. Morningstar's Brian Colello said the market hates uncertainty.

example.setup: Imagine a listed Indian snack company, Crunchy Foods. Its founder-CEO resigns one morning after a scandal, effective immediately. The board must act the same day.

history.text:
The story starts in October 2025. Retail inflation fell to a record-low 0.25% that month, after GST cuts and falling food prices. That low point still matters. Each month's inflation figure compares prices with the same month a year earlier, so a very low starting point makes the next year's figure look bigger.

From June 2026, prices pressed upward. Inflation stayed above 4% for five straight months. Bank of Baroda's Madan Sabnavis points to two causes. A deficient monsoon led to weak sowing of rice, maize, oilseeds, cotton and sugarcane. And he links fuel and LPG price hikes to the war in West Asia.

Growth, meanwhile, held up. On 18 September 2026, the Free Press Journal reported that Moody's had raised India's growth forecast for the year to March 2027 to 7%, from 6%. On 12 November, News18 reported a Moody's raise to 7% from 6.5%. The two sources disagree on the earlier figure. It is not clear whether Moody's raised its forecast once or twice.

By September inflation was 5.54%, close to the 6% ceiling. In October the RBI raised its repo rate to 5.5%. In November, Nandini, Amul and Mother Dairy raised milk prices.

On 12 November the October figure crossed the ceiling: 6.09%. That sets up the RBI's December rate decision.

lesson.concept: How a low base pushes up yearly inflation
lesson.big_idea: Inflation figures compare prices with the same month a year earlier. If prices were unusually low back then, the new figure looks bigger, even if prices rose only a little since.

steps.title: Inflation is a yearly comparison
steps.text: Statisticians price a fixed basket of everyday goods each month: food, fuel, rent, services. Retail inflation is how much that basket's price changed compared with the same month one year earlier, as a percentage.

steps.title: Last year's month is the base
steps.text: The month you compare against is called the base. For October 2026, the base is October 2025, when inflation was a record-low 0.25% after GST cuts and falling food prices.

steps.title: A low base makes a jump
steps.text: If prices were held down in the base month and then recover, the yearly comparison starts from a low point. So the figure looks larger than the recent price pressure alone would suggest.

steps.title: Check if the rise is broad
steps.text: To see past the base, look inside. In October 2026 food inflation was 8.94% and 11 of 12 CPI divisions rose. Sabnavis expects core inflation, which leaves out food and fuel, near 4.5% by year-end.

example.setup: Say a basket of groceries cost ₹100 in October 2024. Cheap vegetables keep it at ₹100 in October 2025. By October 2026 it costs ₹106.

lines.label: Base month price
lines.note: Flat prices mean 0% inflation: a very low base.

lines.label: Yearly inflation, Oct 2026
lines.note: Measured against the low base.

lines.label: Assume a normal base
lines.note: What a typical year's rise might have given.

lines.label: Same price, normal base
lines.note: The same ₹106 now looks much milder.

example.result: The same ₹106 price shows 6% or about 2.9%, depending only on the base. A low base makes yearly inflation look sharper than the recent price pressure behind it.

apply.text: October 2025's 0.25% was a record low, so part of October 2026's 6.09% is the base. How much is not known. But food at 8.94%, rises in 11 of 12 CPI divisions and onions up 116.22% show real pressure. Nayar cites inflation above 6% and growth likely above 7% in calling a December hike almost certain.

practice.q: Say a basket cost ₹200 in October 2025 and ₹210 in October 2026. What is inflation? And what if October 2025 had been ₹205?
practice.answer: First case: ₹210 − ₹200 = ₹10. ₹10 ÷ ₹200 = 5%. Second case: ₹210 − ₹205 = ₹5. ₹5 ÷ ₹205 ≈ 2.4%. The October 2026 price is the same, but the higher base roughly halves the inflation figure.

stories.headline: Government plans special Parliament session to pass the Delimitation Bill
stories.question: Why is the government calling a special Parliament session for the Delimitation Bill?
stories.dek: The government wants another try at redrawing Lok Sabha seats by population, after a key amendment failed in April. It needs two-thirds of MPs voting, and southern states fear losing their voice.

so_far.text: Since 1976, the number of Lok Sabha seats each state gets has been frozen on the 1971 census. On 16 April 2026 the government introduced the Delimitation Bill, 2026, along with the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill. Together they would raise the Lok Sabha's ceiling from 550 to 850 seats. The amendment would also bring in one-third reservation for women. On 17 April the amendment failed, 298 votes to 230. The Delimitation Bill was then marked infructuous, meaning it no longer served any purpose.

what_happened.text: On 12 November 2026, The Hindu reported that the government is planning a special Parliament session to clear the Delimitation Bill. Outlook India reported that Home Minister Amit Shah told Congress leaders a three-day session would be called soon, and that the bills would pass by a margin of 15 to 18 votes. No dates have been officially announced. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said the government had consulted the DMK, SP, Shiv Sena (UBT) and AIMIM. Congress called the plan 'bluster' and wants an all-party meeting first.

steps.text: Changing the Lok Sabha's size needs a constitutional amendment, which must win two-thirds of MPs present and voting.
In April the amendment got 298 votes for and 230 against, short of the two-thirds it needed.
Without the amendment, the Delimitation Bill lost its purpose and was marked infructuous.
Amit Shah reportedly now expects a margin of 15 to 18 votes, and the government has consulted smaller parties.
The Monsoon Session was adjourned on 13 August but never prorogued, so Parliament can be recalled without a fresh summons.

history.text:
Delimitation means redrawing election seats so each one holds roughly the same number of people. India did this in 1952, 1963 and 1973, redrawing seats after each census. Each time, seats followed the new population count.

That stopped in 1976. The 42nd Amendment froze the number of Lok Sabha and assembly seats on 1971 census figures. The aim was that states controlling their population growth would not lose seats.

In 2001 the 84th Amendment extended the freeze until the first census after 2026. The 2002 Delimitation Act allowed only boundary changes inside each state, using the 2001 census. That commission was set up in 2002 and finished in 2008. No state's seat count changed.

Meanwhile, populations drifted apart. Tamil Nadu's fertility fell below replacement level (the rate at which each generation just replaces itself) by the 1990s, yet it kept 39 seats. By 2001 an Uttar Pradesh seat averaged about 2.08 million people, against about 1.59 million in Kerala.

In April 2026 the government brought new bills to redraw seats by population. The key amendment failed on 17 April. On 12 November 2026, reports said a special session is planned to try again.

lesson.concept: How Lok Sabha seats are shared by population
lesson.big_idea: Seats are shared out in proportion to population. If the House grows, a slow-growing state can win more seats yet hold a smaller share, and share is what decides votes.

steps.title: Seats follow headcount
steps.text: Delimitation gives each state seats in proportion to its population, so each MP speaks for roughly the same number of people. India redrew seats this way in 1952, 1963 and 1973, after each census.

steps.title: The freeze stopped the clock
steps.text: In 1976 seat numbers were frozen on the 1971 census. In 2001 the freeze was extended until the first census after 2026. Since then, state populations have grown at different speeds.

steps.title: Unequal votes build up
steps.text: With seats frozen, an MP from a fast-growing state speaks for more people. By 2001 an Uttar Pradesh seat averaged about 2.08 million people; a Kerala seat, about 1.59 million.

steps.title: Count versus share
steps.text: A state's count is its number of seats. Its share is that count divided by the whole House. A bigger House, such as the proposed 850 ceiling, can raise every count while shares still shift.

steps.title: Share decides power
steps.text: Laws pass by majority, and a constitutional amendment needs two-thirds of MPs present and voting. So a group of states' power depends on its share of the House, not its raw count.

example.setup: Imagine a small parliament of 10 seats shared by two states. In 1971, South has 4 million people and North has 6 million. Later, assume South has 5 million and North 10 million.

lines.label: 1971 split
lines.note: 10 million people, so one seat per million.

lines.label: South's old share
lines.note: Its slice of the whole House.

lines.label: New House size
lines.note: Still one seat per million people.

lines.label: New split
lines.note: Both states gain seats.

lines.label: South's new share
lines.note: More seats, but a smaller slice.

example.result: South's count rises from 4 to 5, but its share falls from 40% to about 33%. 'South gains seats' and 'South loses strength' are both true at once.

practice.q: Same two states later (South 5 million, North 10 million), but the House grows to 30 seats. How many seats does South get, and what is its share?
practice.answer: South has 5 of 15 million people, which is one-third. One-third of 30 seats = 10 seats. North gets 20. South's count jumps from 4 to 10, but its share is still about 33%, down from 40%. A bigger House changes counts, not shares.

stories.headline: Kishtwar and Kulgam attacks raise a question: is militancy rising?
stories.question: Do two attacks in two days mean militancy is rising again in Jammu and Kashmir?
stories.dek: Not proven. Three CRPF men were shot in Kulgam on 11 November; two police officers were found shot dead in Kishtwar on 12 November. No official 2026 count was found.

so_far.text: In 2026, Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), a Pakistan-based group, has been the main militant group reported in the forests of the Jammu region, in Kishtwar, Kathua and Udhampur. On 22 February the Army's Operation Trashi-I killed three JeM militants in Passerkut, Chatroo, in Kishtwar. One was preliminarily identified as commander Saifullah, who was linked to a July 2024 attack that killed four soldiers. By that date, seven JeM militants had been killed in Jammu region encounters in 2026.

what_happened.text: On 11 November 2026, at about 2:15 pm IST, attackers on a motorcycle fired at a CRPF checkpoint in Kulgam and fled. Three CRPF men were injured: Rakesh Dass, Santosh Chandru and Somveer Singh. They were taken to hospital in Anantnag; reports differ on whether one was critical. The same day, two Special Police Officers (SPOs), Babi Chand, 57, and Rashpal Kumar, 45, went missing in Kishtwar while travelling to an Army post. Early on 12 November they were found dead with bullet wounds in Kiyar village. Their service weapons were missing. No group has been named for either attack.

steps.text: Large-scale violence has fallen: Wikipedia's table lists 92 deaths in 2025, against 452 in 2018 and 744 in 2007.
But small armed groups remain; in 2026 JeM fighters have been reported in forests in Kishtwar, Kathua and Udhampur.
Hit-and-run attacks need only a few people, like the motorcycle firing in Kulgam, so they can continue when totals are low.
In Kishtwar, the missing service weapons point officials towards militants, but no group has been named or claimed either attack.
So the attacks show danger persists, but without an official 2026 count, a rising trend is unproven.

history.text: The dispute over Jammu and Kashmir goes back to 1947, when India and Pakistan fought their first war over it. For decades after that war, there was no organised insurgency. That changed with the 1987 state election, which was disputed and widely believed to be rigged. The insurgency grew out of it and began in 1989. Violence stayed high for years: Wikipedia's table lists 744 deaths in 2007. In 2016 the killing of Burhan Wani triggered mass protests in which over 100 civilians died, and the table still lists 452 deaths in 2018. In February 2019 a Jaish-e-Mohammad suicide bombing at Pulwama killed 40 CRPF personnel. In August 2019 J&K's special status was revoked, and counter-insurgency operations intensified. By 2025 the table lists 92 deaths, far below the peak. Attacks did not stop, though. In July 2024 an attack killed four soldiers. On 22 April 2025 the Pahalgam attack set off an India–Pakistan crisis. In 2026 the Army has been hunting JeM fighters in the Jammu region's forests.

analogy.text: Think of road crashes on your street. Two crashes in one week feel like a new wave. To know, you compare this year's total with last year's. One bad week inside a quiet year is a cluster, not a trend.
analogy.breaks: Crashes are mostly chance. Attacks are planned by people, so a cluster can signal a real new push and deserves attention.

for_you.text: For most readers in India, the direct effect is small. If you plan to visit J&K, security searches can disrupt movement: after the Kulgam attack, forces added barricades and armoured vehicles and told locals by loudspeaker to stay indoors. The lasting lesson is how to read such news: judge the trend by full-year counts, not by two bad days.

lesson.concept: How to tell a trend from a bad week
lesson.big_idea: A trend means the total over a long period goes up compared with an equal period before. A few attacks close together can happen inside a flat or falling year.

steps.title: Pick one measure
steps.text: Decide what you count and stick to it: attacks, injuries or deaths. Wikipedia's J&K table, for example, counts total insurgency deaths in each year.

steps.title: Compare equal periods
steps.text: Set a full year against a full year, or a month against the same month. By that table, deaths were 744 in 2007, 452 in 2018 and 92 in 2025.

steps.title: Expect clusters by chance
steps.text: Even when the yearly rate stays steady, events do not arrive evenly spaced. Some weeks have none, others have two or three. A cluster alone is not a trend.

steps.title: Don't stretch a week into a year
steps.text: Multiplying one bad week by 52 gives a scary but false yearly figure. Wait for the full count, then work out the change as a percentage of the old total.

steps.title: Check the data exists
steps.text: A trend claim needs a real count. For J&K in 2026, no official fatality tally was found in the sources, so a rise cannot yet be shown from data.

apply.text: The Kulgam firing on 11 November and the Kishtwar deaths found on 12 November are the 'bad week'. They show armed groups can still strike. But the trend depends on the yearly count: Wikipedia's table lists 92 deaths in 2025, far below 744 in 2007, and no official 2026 tally was found.

practice.q: Wikipedia's table lists 452 J&K insurgency deaths in 2018 and 92 in 2025. By roughly what percentage did deaths fall?
practice.answer: Step 1: the fall is 452 − 92 = 360 deaths. Step 2: divide by the starting total: 360 ÷ 452 ≈ 0.8. Step 3: 0.8 is 80%. So deaths fell by about 80%, to roughly one-fifth of the 2018 level.

stories.headline: Trump says US controls Hormuz; Iran threatens bases; oil rebounds
stories.question: Is the US-Iran war heating up again as Trump claims control of Hormuz?
stories.dek: Both sides are making sharper threats, and Iran reports a strike that Oman denies. Oil rose anyway, because traders price the chance of trouble, not only trouble itself.

so_far.text: Iran says it will decide how to negotiate only after seven conditions are met. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio calls those conditions 'unacceptable'. Iran's security council head vowed that no enriched nuclear material will leave Iran. Iran's Assembly of Experts urged considering leaving the NPT, the treaty under which countries promise not to build nuclear weapons. Meanwhile, Iran's army and Revolutionary Guards say tankers that used routes Tehran calls 'unauthorized' hit mines or caught fire.

what_happened.text: In a post reported by CBS News on 11 November, US President Donald Trump said 'we don't need a deal with Iran'. He claimed the US holds Iran's money and controls the Strait of Hormuz. CNBC quoted him: 'We've got their Strait.' In a Veterans Day speech that day, he said ending the war is 'just a question of when we want to end it'. The same day, Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to strike US bases, even in Europe. On 10 November Iran's Fars agency reported a strike on navigation aids on Oman's Didamar Island. Oman denies it. Oil rebounded on 12 November.

steps.text: Trump says the US needs no deal, which signals the standoff over Hormuz could last longer.
Iran replies with threats against US bases, even in Europe, and against islands the US thinks are out of range.
Iran's forces say tankers on routes it calls unauthorized hit mines or caught fire, so shipping risk stays high.
Oil traders price that risk before any barrel is lost, so oil prices rebounded on 12 November.

history.text:
This story starts with geography. Before the war, about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz every day. So did a fifth of its LNG, which is natural gas chilled into liquid for shipping. That narrow channel gave Iran a powerful lever.

On 28 February 2026 the US and Israel attacked Iran. Israel's strike killed Supreme Leader Khamenei, and Iran declared Hormuz closed to shipping. A regional war became a world energy shock.

Around 7–8 April, Pakistan helped broker a fragile ceasefire. The US later launched 'Project Freedom' to escort ships through the strait, trying to keep it open by force.

In mid-June the US and Iran announced a memorandum of understanding. It set out a ceasefire framework and a plan to reopen Hormuz within about 30 days. For a while, diplomacy looked like the way out.

It did not last. On 7 July Iran targeted three commercial vessels in Hormuz. Trump declared the ceasefire 'over', and US bombing of Iran resumed.

Since then, the fight has been over who decides which ships may pass. Iran's army and Guards say tankers on routes Tehran calls 'unauthorized' hit mines or catch fire. Now Trump says the US controls the strait.

lesson.concept: How war risk gets priced into oil
lesson.big_idea: Oil prices reflect what traders expect, not just current supply. When the chance of a shutdown rises, they add a 'risk premium', so prices climb before any barrel is lost.

steps.title: Prices look ahead
steps.text: Traders buy and sell oil for delivery weeks or months away. So the price you see is a bet on future supply, not only on current shipments.

steps.title: Chokepoints concentrate the risk
steps.text: A chokepoint is a narrow route that many cargoes must use. Before the war, about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil passed through Hormuz daily. A shutdown there would send prices far higher.

steps.title: Chance times damage
steps.text: Traders blend two worlds: a calm price and a crisis price, each weighted by how likely it is. The extra above the calm price is the risk premium.

steps.title: Words move the odds
steps.text: Talk of peace lowers the chance of crisis. Talk of 'no deal' or new strikes raises it. So prices can move when no tanker is stopped, as on 12 November.

steps.title: Higher price, bigger bill
steps.text: Importers pay the higher price. A former NITI Aayog chief estimated every $10-a-barrel rise can add $13–14 billion to India's import bill.

example.setup: Suppose oil costs $60 a barrel in a calm world and would jump to $110 if Hormuz shut. Assume traders see a 20% chance of that shutdown.

lines.label: Calm-world part
lines.note: An 80% chance that nothing goes wrong.

lines.label: Crisis part
lines.note: A small chance, but a big price.

lines.label: Price traders pay
lines.note: $10 above the calm price: that is the risk premium.

lines.label: Odds double to 40%
lines.note: Same oil, higher odds, price up another $10.

lines.label: India's extra bill
lines.note: Using the former NITI Aayog chief's estimate.

example.result: No barrel was lost, yet the price rose from $70 to $80 because the odds of trouble doubled. Words that change the odds change the price, and can swell India's import bill.

apply.text: On 12 November oil rebounded after Trump said no deal was needed and 'we've got their Strait'. In lesson terms, 'no deal' raises the odds of a long fight over a route that carried a quarter of seaborne oil. Rezaei's threats and the disputed Didamar strike point the same way. No barrel had to be lost for prices to rise.

practice.q: Same oil: calm price $60, crisis price $110. Peace talks cut the shutdown chance to 5%. What price do traders pay, and what is the risk premium?
practice.answer: Calm part: 95% × $60 = $57. Crisis part: 5% × $110 = $5.50. Price: $57 + $5.50 = $62.50. Risk premium: $62.50 − $60 = $2.50, a quarter of the $10 premium at a 20% chance.

stories.headline: Fed officials weigh faster rate hikes after hot October prices
stories.question: Why are Fed officials now talking about faster rate hikes, and who else is following?
stories.dek: October prices rose faster than expected, and several Fed officials say rates are still too low to cool them. Britain has already hiked, and Europe's central bank may follow in December.

so_far.text: On 28 February 2026 the US and Israel struck Iran. Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, and energy prices jumped. The Fed, America's central bank, raised rates in September. On 28 October it held its target range at 3.75–4%, with two officials voting for a hike. On 10 November the October price report showed US prices up 0.4% in a single month.

what_happened.text: After a hot October price report, Fed officials are openly discussing more and bigger rate hikes. On 10 November, Governor Christopher Waller said he leans toward a quarter-point December hike, but a half-point should be considered if core prices rose near or above 0.3%. They rose 0.3%. In remarks reported on 11 November, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan called for at least two quarter-point hikes, possibly faster this winter. Kansas City Fed's Jeffrey Schmid called rates 'quite accommodative'. Governor Bowman saw 'still work to do' but did not call more hikes a given. Abroad, the Bank of England raised its rate to 4% on 5 November.

steps.text: The Iran war effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices sharply higher.
Energy costs are now seeping into other prices; even core prices rose 0.3% in October alone.
With rates at 3.75–4%, some officials say borrowing is still too cheap to cool spending.
So they want more or bigger hikes, to raise borrowing costs before high inflation settles in.
The same energy shock hit Britain and Europe: the Bank of England hiked in November, and the ECB hiked in June.

history.text: The Fed's last rate hike before this cycle came in July 2023. In 2025 it went the other way, with 'insurance' cuts totalling three-quarters of a point. Then, on 28 February 2026, the US and Israel struck Iran. Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carries about a fifth of the world's oil and gas. By mid-April the International Energy Agency called it the 'most severe oil supply shock in history', and US petrol cost $4.11 a gallon. The European Central Bank (ECB) moved first. In June it lifted its rate to 2.25% from 2%, the first major central bank to hike in this shock. By early September oil had eased from peaks above $100 but stayed well above pre-war levels. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said underlying inflation had not meaningfully improved. On 15–16 September the Fed raised rates for the first time since July 2023. On 28 October it held at 3.75–4%, but Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted for a hike. The same day Warsh said that from autumn 2027 one of the Fed's eight yearly meetings, a calendar used since 1981, will have no rate vote. On 5 November the Bank of England raised its key rate to 4%. So by the time October's hot price data arrived, the Fed was already leaning toward tightening, and its peers were moving too.

lesson.concept: How the real interest rate shows if rates bite
lesson.big_idea: An interest rate only slows spending if it is higher than inflation. The gap between the two, the 'real' rate, tells you whether a central bank's policy is loose or tight.

steps.title: The rate is the starting price
steps.text: A central bank sets a short-term interest rate. The Fed's target range is now 3.75–4%. Banks build their loan and deposit rates on top of it, so it is the starting price of borrowing.

steps.title: Inflation eats into it
steps.text: Inflation is how fast prices rise. When prices rise, the money a borrower repays later buys less than the money they borrowed. So inflation quietly cuts the true cost of a loan.

steps.title: Real rate: rate minus inflation
steps.text: Subtract the inflation rate from the interest rate. The answer is the 'real' rate. It tells you what borrowing truly costs once rising prices are counted.

steps.title: Loose or tight
steps.text: A real rate near zero or below is 'accommodative', meaning loose: it encourages borrowing and spending. A real rate well above zero is 'restrictive', meaning tight: it cools spending and, over months, prices.

steps.title: Bigger steps, faster squeeze
steps.text: If inflation runs close to the rate, a central bank can raise it in quarter-point or half-point steps. Bigger steps lift the real rate sooner, but rate changes take time to show their effects.

apply.text: The Fed's range is 3.75–4%. October core prices rose 0.3% in one month; repeated for twelve months, that is about 3.6% a year. One month is not a trend, but it puts the real rate near zero. That is why Schmid calls rates 'quite accommodative', Waller says policy is 'not as restrictive as I had thought', and Logan wants at least two hikes.

practice.q: Same ₹1,00,000 loan, but the rate is 5.5% and prices rise 4%. What is the real rate, and are you ahead?
practice.answer: Interest: 5.5% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹5,500, so you get back ₹1,05,500. Shopping now costs ₹1,00,000 + 4% = ₹1,04,000. You are ahead by ₹1,500. Real rate: 5.5% − 4% = 1.5%. Above zero, so this rate is restrictive: it rewards saving over borrowing.

stories.headline: Indonesia's vice-president Gibran resigns after court rulings on his diplomas
stories.question: Why did Indonesia's vice-president, the former president's son, suddenly resign?
stories.dek: Gibran Rakabuming Raka quit on 12 November 2026 after court rulings questioned his school certificates. He calls it personal. President Prabowo links it to the rulings. Indonesia's top assembly must elect a successor.

so_far.text: Gibran Rakabuming Raka is the son of Joko Widodo, or Jokowi, Indonesia's former president. In 2024 he ran for vice-president as Prabowo Subianto's running mate. They won with almost 59% of the vote, and Gibran was sworn in on 20 October 2024. Candidates must meet a minimum secondary-education requirement. Since September 2025 a lawsuit has questioned his school papers. The BBC reports a growing rift between Prabowo and Jokowi.

what_happened.text: On 12 November 2026 Gibran submitted his resignation to the MPR, Indonesia's top legislative body. MPR Speaker Ahmad Muzani declared the vice-presidency vacant. The MPR said the letter gave no reason. Gibran said the decision was personal and had nothing to do with his diploma. President Prabowo said two court rulings showed "discrepancies or shortcomings" in meeting constitutional requirements, so Gibran stepped down for the nation's sake. The two had met for over two hours the day before. The rupiah fell as much as 0.6% to a record low of 18,255 per dollar.

steps.text: To stand in 2024, a candidate had to prove a minimum secondary-education level with documents.
Courts found no proof of a high-school-equivalent diploma, and the Supreme Court voided his conversion certificate.
That left a sitting vice-president whose eligibility for the 2024 election was in legal doubt.
An appeal looked weak: the legal affairs minister said the Supreme Court ruling is final.
Gibran resigned, calling it personal; Prabowo said he stepped down for the nation's sake.

history.text:
Indonesians elect a president and a vice-president together, as a pair. Vice-presidents almost never quit: before Gibran, the last to resign was Mohammad Hatta, in 1956.

Gibran's story starts with his studies. He attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore. He enrolled at UTS Insearch in Australia but did not continue. He later earned an MDIS diploma in 2010 and a marketing degree via the University of Bradford.

The first turning point came on 17 October 2023. Candidates had to be at least 40; Gibran was 36. The Constitutional Court, led by Anwar Usman, Gibran's uncle by marriage, added an exception for people elected as regional leaders. That opened the door for him to run. The election commission was later found to have breached ethics.

Next, Gibran won and was sworn in on 20 October 2024. The New York Times calls him a symbol of the partnership that brought Prabowo to power.

In September 2025 the focus moved from his age to his education. A citizen sued, alleging his UTS Insearch diploma was fake. In October 2026 the Constitutional Court found no proof of a high-school-equivalent diploma. It refused to disqualify him only because the person suing lacked standing, the legal right to bring the case. The Supreme Court later voided his conversion certificate. His eligibility was now in doubt, and on 12 November 2026 he resigned.

lesson.concept: How Indonesia replaces a vice-president mid-term
lesson.big_idea: A vice-president must meet set requirements to hold office. If the post becomes empty, there is no new national vote: the president proposes two names and the MPR elects one within 60 days.

steps.title: Candidates must meet entry rules
steps.text: To run, a candidate must meet constitutional requirements, such as a minimum age of 40 and a minimum secondary-education level. Each must be proven with documents. In 2023 the Constitutional Court added an age exception for elected regional leaders.

steps.title: Courts can test the documents
steps.text: If someone challenges the papers, courts examine them. In Gibran's case the Constitutional Court found no proof of a high-school-equivalent diploma. The Supreme Court voided his conversion certificate, a ruling the legal affairs minister calls final.

steps.title: A resignation makes a vacancy
steps.text: A vice-president can resign by letter to the MPR, the People's Consultative Assembly, Indonesia's top legislative body. Its Speaker then declares the post vacant. Nobody steps in automatically, and there is no new public vote.

steps.title: The president names two
steps.text: The president nominates two candidates and sends them to the MPR. Only these two can be elected, so the president shapes the choice while the assembly makes the final pick.

steps.title: The MPR checks and votes
steps.text: The MPR verifies both candidates' documents, then holds a plenary vote, meaning all members vote together in one sitting. The whole process must be completed within 60 days.

apply.text: So when Gibran resigned on 12 November 2026, the MPR declared the post vacant. Prabowo will now send two names. The MPR will check their documents and hold a plenary vote within 60 days, which points to around 11 January 2027. Indonesians will not vote again for this post.

practice.q: Suppose the vacancy starts on 12 November. Counting 60 days, roughly when must the MPR have elected a new vice-president?
practice.answer: Count step by step. 12 November to 30 November is 18 days. December adds 31 days, making 49. You need 11 more days, which lands on 11 January. So the MPR has until about 11 January 2027.

stories.headline: Trump–Xi Shenzhen meeting: a fragile trade truce and Taiwan at stake
stories.question: What is at stake when Trump and Xi meet in Shenzhen on 18–19 November?
stories.dek: A one-year trade truce cut US tariffs on Chinese goods, and it is due to expire in January. Shenzhen may decide whether it lasts. Six days earlier, Xi called Taiwan's reunification certain.

so_far.text: On 30 October 2025 in Busan, Trump and Xi agreed a one-year trade truce. The US halved its fentanyl-linked tariff from 20% to 10%. That cut the overall tariff on Chinese goods from 57% to 47%. China suspended its October 2025 rare-earth export controls and resumed buying US farm goods. AP calls the truce fragile and says it is due to expire in January. Trump and Xi are expected to meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18–19 November 2026. It would be their third meeting this year.

what_happened.text: On 12 November Xi Jinping said at the Great Hall of the People that 'the complete reunification of the motherland must be realised, and it will certainly be realised.' He called resolving the Taiwan question the Communist Party's 'unwavering historical mission'. DW reports he did not mention military force. Taiwan quickly rejected Beijing's demands. On 11 November, at China's request, foreign minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke by phone before the summit. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer pressed Vice Premier He Lifeng on rare earths, critical minerals and farm purchases.

steps.text: At Busan in October 2025, the US cut tariffs; China paused rare-earth controls and resumed US farm purchases.
That truce is due to expire in January, so both sides need an extension or a new deal.
Each side holds a lever: CNBC reports calls in Washington for tighter AI-chip limits, and Beijing signalling rare-earth curbs in reply.
Xi's Taiwan speech on 12 November, six days before the summit, restated the Party's 'unwavering historical mission'.
The US says leader-level talks matter; China called the call 'positive and constructive'. Only Washington's account mentions denuclearisation.

history.text: The Taiwan dispute began in 1949. The Communists won China's civil war and founded the People's Republic of China. The losing Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan. From then on, two governments each claimed to be China. The world then shifted towards Beijing. In 1971 the People's Republic replaced the Republic of China at the UN. In 1979 the US switched its diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing. In 1992 the two sides reached the '1992 Consensus'. Both accepted 'one China', but each kept its own meaning of it. That vague deal let them talk. In March 2005 China passed the Anti-Secession Law, authorising military action if Taiwan formally declares independence. In 2016 Taiwan's president Tsai Ing-wen did not accept the 1992 Consensus, and Beijing suspended official communications. In 2022, after Nancy Pelosi's visit, China's army held large live-fire drills around Taiwan. Wikipedia calls this the start of the Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis. Trade became a second front. On 30 October 2025 at Busan, Trump and Xi agreed a one-year truce. The US lowered tariffs, and China paused rare-earth controls and resumed farm purchases.

lesson.concept: How stacked tariffs and a timed truce work
lesson.big_idea: A tariff is a tax on imports, and US tariffs on China come in layers that add up. A truce removes part of a layer in return for concessions, but only until its end date.

steps.title: A tariff is an import tax
steps.text: A tariff is a tax charged when goods cross a border. It is a percentage of the goods' value. The importing company pays it first, and often passes it on in prices.

steps.title: Layers add up
steps.text: US tariffs on Chinese goods are stacked in layers, each added for a different reason. Before Busan, the fentanyl-linked layer was 20%, and all layers together came to 57%. So the other layers made up 37%.

steps.title: A truce cuts a layer
steps.text: At Busan on 30 October 2025, the US halved the fentanyl layer to 10%, so the total fell to 47%. In return, China suspended rare-earth controls and resumed US farm purchases.

steps.title: A truce has an end date
steps.text: The truce is due to expire in January. Until then, each side keeps its tools ready. CNBC reports Beijing could tighten rare-earth controls if tougher US chip laws pass.

practice.q: Say a US shop imports Chinese goods worth $500. How much less tariff does it pay after Busan than before?
practice.answer: Before: 57% of $500 = $285. After: 47% of $500 = $235. Saving: $285 − $235 = $50. Check: that is just the 10-point fentanyl cut, 10% of $500 = $50.

scenes.say: Ab woh idea jo seekhna hai: stacked tariffs aur timed truce kaise kaam karte hain. Tariff ek tax hai jo border paar karte waqt goods par lagta hai, unki value ke percent ke hisaab se. Pehle importer bharta hai, aur aksar daam badhakar customers par daal deta hai.
scenes.speak: अब वो idea जो सीखना है: stacked tariffs और timed truce कैसे काम करते हैं। Tariff एक tax है जो border पार करते वक़्त goods पर लगता है, उनकी value के percent के हिसाब से। पहले importer भरता है, और अक्सर दाम बढ़ाकर customers पर डाल देता है।

scenes.say: China par American tariffs layers mein aate hain. Har layer alag wajah se lagi, aur sab jud jaati hain. Busan se pehle fentanyl layer 20 percent thi aur total 57, toh baaki layers milkar 37 hui. Truce ek layer kaat deta hai, lekin sirf uski end date tak.
scenes.speak: China पर American tariffs layers में आते हैं। हर layer अलग वजह से लगी, और सब जुड़ जाती हैं। Busan से पहले fentanyl layer 20 percent थी और total 57, तो बाक़ी layers मिलकर 37 हुईं। Truce एक layer काट देता है, लेकिन सिर्फ़ उसकी end date तक।

scenes.say: Chaliye ek example lete hain. Maan lijiye ek American toy shop China se 1000 dollar ke khilone mangwati hai. Busan se pehle, 57 percent par, tariff tha 570 dollar. Usmein se 200 dollar fentanyl layer ka tha. Busan ne woh layer aadhi karke 100 dollar kar di.
scenes.speak: चलिए एक example लेते हैं। मान लीजिए एक American toy shop China से 1000 dollar के खिलौने मँगवाती है। Busan से पहले, 57 percent पर, tariff था 570 dollar। उसमें से 200 dollar fentanyl layer का था। Busan ने वो layer आधी करके 100 dollar कर दी।

scenes.say: Toh naya bill: 370 plus 100, matlab 470 dollar. Yeh hua 47 percent. Shop ko har 1000 par 100 dollar ki bachat. Ab sochiye truce lapse ho jaata hai aur woh layer phir 20 percent ho jaati hai. Bill wapas 570 par pahunch jaata hai.
scenes.speak: तो नया bill: 370 plus 100, मतलब 470 dollar। यह हुआ 47 percent। Shop को हर 1000 पर 100 dollar की बचत। अब सोचिए truce lapse हो जाता है और वो layer फिर 20 percent हो जाती है। Bill वापस 570 पर पहुँच जाता है।

scenes.say: Ab kaun kya keh raha hai. Xi kehte hain reunification hona hi chahiye aur hoga. Taiwan ki Mainland Affairs Council one country, two systems ko Communist Party ke raaj ke aage jhukna maanti hai. Spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh ne kaha ki wording pehle se zyada alag nahi hai. Toh Taiwan ki apni reading mein yeh koi nayi line nahi thi, aur DW kehta hai Xi ne force ka zikr nahi kiya.
scenes.show: Taiwan: 'not much different from the past'
scenes.speak: अब कौन क्या कह रहा है। Xi कहते हैं reunification होना ही चाहिए और होगा। Taiwan की Mainland Affairs Council one country, two systems को Communist Party के राज के आगे झुकना मानती है। Spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh ने कहा कि wording पहले से ज़्यादा अलग नहीं है। तो Taiwan की अपनी reading में यह कोई नई line नहीं थी, और DW कहता है Xi ने force का ज़िक्र नहीं किया।

scenes.say: Trade par Treasury Secretary Bessent kehte hain ki America ko zyada woh banana chahiye jo woh consume karta hai, aur China ko zyada woh consume karna chahiye jo woh banata hai. Woh ise reciprocity kehte hain, hostility nahi. State Department ke mutabik Rubio aur Wang sahmat hue ki leader-level baatcheet zaroori hai. China ne call ko positive aur constructive bataya. Denuclearisation ka zikr sirf Washington ke account mein tha.
scenes.speak: Trade पर Treasury Secretary Bessent कहते हैं कि America को ज़्यादा वो बनाना चाहिए जो वो consume करता है, और China को ज़्यादा वो consume करना चाहिए जो वो बनाता है। वो इसे reciprocity कहते हैं, hostility नहीं। State Department के मुताबिक Rubio और Wang सहमत हुए कि leader-level बातचीत ज़रूरी है। China ने call को positive और constructive बताया। Denuclearisation का ज़िक्र सिर्फ़ Washington के account में था।

views.view: US should produce more; China should consume more
Rubio call was 'positive and constructive'
Leader-level talks matter for peace and denuclearization

scenes.say: Ab sawaal, India mein aapke liye iska kya matlab hai? 2025 mein Vajiram and Ravi aur Tribune India ki commentary ne kaha ki US-China truce factories ko China se India shift karne ki koshish ko kamzor kar sakta hai. scenes.say: Ab lesson apply kijiye. Agar Shenzhen mein truce extend hota hai, toh 47 percent ka rate bana reh sakta hai. America ko rare earths, minerals aur farm purchases chahiye. Aur CNBC ke mutabik, agar America mein chips par sakht kanoon paas hote hain, toh Beijing rare-earth curbs tight kar sakta hai.
scenes.speak: अब lesson apply कीजिए। अगर Shenzhen में truce extend होता है, तो 47 percent का rate बना रह सकता है। America को rare earths, minerals और farm purchases चाहिए। और CNBC के मुताबिक, अगर America में chips पर सख़्त क़ानून पास होते हैं, तो Beijing rare-earth curbs tight कर सकता है।

Woh truce January mein khatam hone wala hai, aur Xi ne 12 November ko Taiwan par apna daava doharaya. 18 aur 19 November ko Shenzhen par nazar rakhiye.

stories.headline: Rich countries' climate finance pledges fall 71% as COP31 talks harden
stories.question: Why have rich countries' climate finance pledges shrunk, and what does it mean at COP31?
stories.dek: Most multi-year pledges ran out in 2025 and few were renewed, so pledged public money fell about 71%. That leaves week two of COP31 fighting over finance with little new money.

so_far.text: COP31, the UN's yearly climate summit, runs from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya. Türkiye hosts, with Murat Kurum as COP President. Australia's Chris Bowen presides over the negotiations. On 9 November the opening session adopted a separate agenda item for a Climate Finance Work Programme, over EU objections. India had pushed for it. On 10 November UN Secretary-General António Guterres attacked oil companies' profits.

what_happened.text: On 11 November, Carbon Brief published an analysis of donor pledges. Developed countries' public climate-finance pledges for developing nations fell about 71%, from roughly $40bn a year to about $11.7bn a year for the rest of the 2020s. Most multi-year pledges expired without replacements; only five donors have announced new ones. EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra was quoted, via Bloomberg, saying any conversation on new fresh money is 'dead in the water'. On 12 November the World Leaders' Summit closed. Over $480m was announced for methane and other non-CO2 gases, but no joint declaration was found.

steps.text: Most donors made multi-year pledges that ended in 2025, and most have not announced new ones.
The US left the Paris Agreement and cut aid; it had committed $11.4bn a year under Biden and now gives nothing official.
European governments cut aid budgets for defence and economic strain, as politics shifted in Germany, France, Spain and Sweden.
With only five donors renewing, the total sinks far below the $300bn-by-2035 goal, so finance talks at COP31 get harder.

history.text: The root is the UN climate treaty, the UNFCCC, adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. Its rule of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' says all countries act, but developed countries take the lead. The 1997 Kyoto Protocol built on that treaty. In 2009 developed countries pledged to mobilise $100bn a year for developing nations by 2020. This was formalised at Cancún in 2010, turning the duty to lead into a number. The 2015 Paris Agreement extended the $100bn goal through 2025. The goal was missed in 2020 ($83.3bn) and 2021 ($89.6bn), and first met in 2022, per the OECD. At COP29 in Baku in 2024, countries set a bigger goal: at least $300bn a year by 2035, with no separate goal for adaptation. COP30 in Belém in 2025 called for tripling adaptation finance by 2035, without a number, and set up a two-year finance work programme. Then, in 2025, most donors' multi-year pledges expired, without new ones to replace them.

lesson.concept: How expiring pledges shrink the climate finance pot
lesson.big_idea: A collective climate goal is a target for all rich countries together. The real money comes from each country's own pledge, which has an end date. When pledges expire and are not renewed, the total falls.

steps.title: The goal is shared
steps.text: At COP29 in Baku in 2024, countries agreed a goal of at least $300bn a year by 2035. It is collective: it does not tell any single country how much to pay.

steps.title: Each donor pledges separately
steps.text: The actual money comes from each donor's own pledge: an amount per year, up to an end year. Germany and France, for example, pledged €6bn a year by 2025 and set nothing beyond it.

steps.title: Pledges run out
steps.text: A multi-year pledge covers several years, then stops. If the country announces no new pledge, its money simply drops out of the total. Most pledges ended in 2025.

steps.title: Add live pledges, compare goal
steps.text: To see future money, add up only the pledges still running. Carbon Brief did this and got about $11.7bn a year. The gap to the goal is what negotiators fight over.

apply.text: Carbon Brief's figures follow this pattern. Pledges fell from about $40bn to about $11.7bn a year because most expired in 2025, and the US, Germany, France and co-host Australia have nothing new. NRDC's Joe Thwaites says the lack of new pledges makes finance talks tougher. India wants a formal finance work programme, while Hoekstra says new money is 'dead in the water'.

practice.q: Same four countries, but country B renews its pledge at $5bn a year from 2026. What is the new total, and how big is the fall?
practice.answer: Live pledges in 2026: D's $10bn plus B's $5bn = $15bn. Money lost: $40bn − $15bn = $25bn. Fall: $25bn ÷ $40bn = 62.5%. One smaller renewal softens the fall from 75% to 62.5%.

stories.headline: Spain's first general strike since 2012 is about rent
stories.question: Why did millions in Spain strike over housing costs for the first time in 14 years?
stories.dek: Spain is short about 750,000 homes, and average rent nearly equals a young worker's pay. After parliament blocked rent and eviction curbs, unions struck before a 29 November election.

so_far.text: Spain is short of about 750,000 homes, a gap its central bank expects to pass one million by 2028. Average rent is €1,176, about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary, says the Youth Council of Spain. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's party, PSOE, lacks a majority. After parliament rejected government housing decrees in October 2026, he called a snap election for 29 November. Protests grew after an 87-year-old Madrid woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted and later died.

what_happened.text: On 11 November 2026, Spain held its first nationwide 24-hour general strike since 2012, backed by the two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, and tenants' groups. Unions said about 4 million workers joined. France 24 reported tens of thousands marching, and business leaders played down participation. Unions reported about 90% participation at ports and in carmaking, with total stoppages at Volkswagen in Navarre and SEAT in Barcelona. Electricity demand fell by up to 15.5% in one hour. Police reported 40 arrests from 476 incidents; 20 protesters were injured.

steps.text: Spain has about 750,000 fewer homes than it needs, and its central bank expects the gap to pass one million by 2028.
With too few homes, households compete and rents rise: average rent, €1,176, now equals about 98.7% of a young person's pay.
Government decrees to curb evictions and limit rent rises failed in parliament in October 2026, because Sánchez's party lacks a majority.
Anger grew after an 87-year-old Madrid woman, Maricarmen Abascal, died following her eviction.
The two largest unions and tenants' groups turned that anger into the first nationwide 24-hour strike since 2012.

history.text: Spain's housing story begins with a boom. Around 2001 a property bubble started, and it peaked in 2007. A crash followed, lasting from 2008 to 2014. In July 2008 the developer Martinsa-Fadesa went bankrupt with debts above €7 billion, the largest suspension of payments in Spain's economic history. Then the crash hit lenders. In 2012 the state nationalised, or took over, several savings banks, including Bankia in May 2012. That same year unions held a general strike against austerity during the euro zone debt crisis. It was the last general strike until November 2026, which is why the new one is the first in 14 years. By the end of 2013, prices had fallen about 45% from 2007, according to one source. The rules on losing a home also came under the spotlight: EU courts ruled in 2013 and 2014 that Spain's eviction and mortgage laws breached EU consumer protections. By 2026 the problem had changed shape. It was no longer falling prices but high rents: long-term rents hit a record €15 per square metre in April 2026. In October 2026 parliament rejected government decrees to curb evictions and limit rent rises, and Sánchez called a snap election.

lesson.concept: How a housing shortage pushes rents up
lesson.big_idea: When more households want homes than there are homes, they compete, and landlords can raise rents. Rent then takes a bigger share of pay, leaving less for everything else.

steps.title: Count homes against households
steps.text: Compare how many households need a home with how many homes exist. If households outnumber homes, the gap is a housing deficit. Spain's is about 750,000 homes, heading past one million by 2028.

steps.title: A shortage becomes bidding
steps.text: With too few homes, families compete for each one. A landlord with several applicants can ask for more rent and still find a tenant. Wages are not set this way, so rents can rise faster than pay.

steps.title: Measure the squeeze on pay
steps.text: Divide monthly rent by monthly pay to get the rent-to-income share. In Spain, average rent of €1,176 is about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary, per the Youth Council of Spain.

steps.title: Supply catches up slowly
steps.text: Building homes takes years. If fewer homes are built than new households form, the deficit grows each year, and the pressure on rents stays.

steps.title: Two kinds of fix
steps.text: Governments can protect tenants by limiting rent rises and evictions, or add supply by building more. Spain's parliament rejected the first kind in October 2026; the CEOE business lobby wants the second, plus tax cuts.

example.setup: Imagine a small town with 100 flats and 110 families who each need one. Rent is €500 a month, and a young worker there earns €1,000 a month.

example.result: Ten missing flats pushed rent from half of pay to 60%, leaving €400 instead of €500. Spain is missing about 750,000 homes, and young people's rent is about 98.7% of pay.

practice.q: Same town, but 20 more families arrive and rent climbs to €800 a month. Pay stays at €1,000. What share of pay is rent, and what is left?
practice.answer: Rent share: €800 ÷ €1,000 = 80% of pay. Left over: €1,000 − €800 = €200. The worker keeps €200 for everything else, half of the €400 they had when rent was €600.

check.q: Why can a housing shortage make rents rise faster than wages?
options: Households compete for too few homes, so landlords can charge more, while pay is set elsewhere
Tourist flats now make up most of Spain's homes
Strikes force landlords to raise rents to cover their losses
check.why: Rent is set by competition for scarce homes. Wages don't depend on that, so a shortage lifts rent without lifting pay.

Families boli lagati hain, aur rent badhta hai, maan lijiye 20 percent, 600 euro tak. Ab yeh salary ka 60 percent hai.
scenes.speak: मान लीजिए एक town है जिसमें 100 flats और 110 families हैं। 10 families को घर नहीं मिलता। Rent है 500 euro। एक young worker कमाता है 1000 euro। यानी salary का आधा। Families बोली लगाती हैं, और rent बढ़ता है, मान लीजिए 20 percent, 600 euro तक। अब यह salary का 60 percent है।

scenes.say: Toh worker ke paas baaki sab ke liye bachte hain 400 euro. Sirf 10 flats ki kami ne rent ko salary ke aadhe se 60 percent tak pahuncha diya. Ab aap khud try kijiye: agar rent 800 euro ho jaaye, toh salary ka kitna hissa? 80 percent, aur bachenge sirf 200 euro.
scenes.speak: तो worker के पास बाकी सब के लिए बचते हैं 400 euro। सिर्फ 10 flats की कमी ने rent को salary के आधे से 60 percent तक पहुँचा दिया। अब आप खुद try कीजिए: अगर rent 800 euro हो जाए, तो salary का कितना हिस्सा? 80 percent, और बचेंगे सिर्फ 200 euro।

scenes.say: Do nazariye hain. Madrid Tenants Union ki Alicia del Rio kehti hain ki jab tak housing model upar se neeche tak nahi badalta, movement nahi rukega. CEOE ki Angela de Miguel strike ko counterproductive kehti hain. Woh chahti hain ki zyada ghar banein, aur construction aur kharidari par tax kam ho.
scenes.speak: दो नज़रिए हैं। Madrid Tenants Union की Alicia del Rio कहती हैं कि जब तक housing model ऊपर से नीचे तक नहीं बदलता, movement नहीं रुकेगा। CEOE की Angela de Miguel strike को counterproductive कहती हैं। वो चाहती हैं कि ज़्यादा घर बनें, और construction और खरीदारी पर tax कम हो।

scenes.say: India mein aapke liye prices, loan EMIs ya jobs par koi seedha asar nahi hai. Lekin sabak saaf hai: ghar kam hon, toh rent salary se tez badhta hai. Ek baat aur. Zyadatar Spanish log rent ke liye tourist flats ko zimmedaar maante hain. Par ek report ke mutabik woh sirf kareeb ek point do chaar percent ghar hain, jo pehle ek point chaar ek the.
scenes.speak: India में आपके लिए prices, loan EMIs या jobs पर कोई सीधा असर नहीं है। लेकिन सबक साफ है: घर कम हों, तो rent salary से तेज़ बढ़ता है। एक बात और। ज़्यादातर Spanish लोग rent के लिए tourist flats को ज़िम्मेदार मानते हैं। पर एक report के मुताबिक वो सिर्फ करीब एक point दो चार percent घर हैं, जो पहले एक point चार एक थे।

scenes.say: Aage kya hoga? Spain 29 November ko snap election mein vote karega. Polls mein far right aage hai, aur reports ke mutabik Sanchez housing ke mudde par voters ko jodne ki koshish kar rahe hain. Yeh baatein ab bhi saaf nahi: strike par sarkar ka jawab, official turnout, aur kya rent aur eviction limits wapas aayengi.
scenes.speak: आगे क्या होगा? Spain 29 November को snap election में vote करेगा। Polls में far right आगे है, और reports के मुताबिक Sanchez housing के मुद्दे पर voters को जोड़ने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं। यह बातें अब भी साफ नहीं: strike पर सरकार का जवाब, official turnout, और क्या rent और eviction limits वापस आएँगी।

scenes.say: Teen baatein yaad rakhiye. Ek: jab households gharon se zyada hon, toh rent salary se tez badh sakta hai. Do: 2012 ke baad Spain ki pehli general strike aise rent ke khilaaf thi jo young logon ki salary ke lagbhag barabar hai. Teen: 29 November ke election par nazar rakhiye.

scenes.speak: तीन बातें याद रखिए। एक: जब households घरों से ज़्यादा हों, तो rent salary से तेज़ बढ़ सकता है। दो: 2012 के बाद Spain की पहली general strike ऐसे rent के खिलाफ थी जो young लोगों की salary के लगभग बराबर है। तीन: 29 November के election पर नज़र रखिए।
